newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Bel-20 index to trek up again, Colruyt a star.
newsitem.headline: Bel-20 index to trek up again, Colruyt a star.

text.p: The Bel-20 index of leading shares is expected to continue its record-breaking flight into outer space with no crash landing expected due to the Amsterdam summit on Monday and Tuesday, analysts said on Friday.

"I have this uneasy feeling because this euphoria is fairly negative but then again, rates are still low, the dollar is strong, there is plenty of cash and companies perform well. All elements are positive, and there is no alternative (for shares)," said Stefan Casteleyn at Antwerp brokerage Corluy.
A weaker-than-forecast May U.S. PPI report followed by fresh gains on Wall Street provided additonal support for the Bel-20.
The producer price data confirmed that price rises in the U.S. are under control and gave the view that U.S. interest rates are to remain stable for now a firmer base.
The Bel-20 ended 0.38 percent higher at a record 2,400.36 points after it earlier set a new intraday high at 2,410.80.
Dealers and analysts shrugged off fears of a major correction in the near future.
"We're not on the eve of a crash," Casteleyn said. But the summer holiday period would be more than welcome. "We do need a cooling off period, it has all gone up too fast."

Dealers said they were surprised by the fresh gains of retailer Colruyt. The share ended 3.4 percent higher at 16,800, after earlier shooting to 17,000, bringing its total gain this week to 16 percent.

Colruyt's dash started when players suddenly realised the retailer had lagged the market in recent months. The shock was triggered by notification Colruyt would publish full 1996/1997 earnings on June 26. Rumours Colruyt might sell its Dolmen Computer unit contributed to the buying spree.
Colruyt later said it would split Dolmen into two units but had no plans to sell it.
"The value per share of Dolmen for Colruyt is 1,000 francs at most, but Colruyt has already gone up 2,000 francs," Casteleyn noted.
The fairy tale of this week's other star, chemicals and pharmaceuticals firm UCB, ended abruptly, at least for now, when it shed 3.6 percent to 115,000 francs.
Generale Bank said UCB's rise had been fuelled by comments earlier this week by CEO Georges Jacobs, who woke up players after the share had remained steady at 95,000 francs for several months.

Jacobs said that after an increase in ordinary pre-tax profits by 33 percent, UCB was likely to see a similar increase in 1997. That news, together with an announcement that a share split was being considered, propelled the stock, and the index with it, to record highs.
UCB was still quoted at 26,825 francs on June 13, 1995, and at 58,750 francs exactly one year ago.
But dealers said UCB was now too expensive and had totally run out of steam.
